43007515.resumo: Pediatric cerebral malaria (PCM) kills 15% to 25% of the African children in whom it is diagnosed and leaves many survivors with neurocognitive deficits. It is a disease of the cerebral microvasculature whose pathogenic sequence is now partly resolved at the molecular level. Plasmodium falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 binds a broad range of endothelial cell receptors, of which binding to the endothelial protein C receptor, in some cases together with intercellular adhesion molecule 1, is the combination linked to severe and cerebral disease. CD36 is the receptor most commonly used by field isolates but is associated with uncomplicated malaria, at least two dozen further receptors have been described for parasitized erythrocytes, and a PfEMP1 binding domain has been identified for only a few of them. The ensuing endothelial activation releases von Willebrand factor and angiopoietin-2 and disables Tie - 2 signaling. Free heme, delivered in part by histidine-rich protein 2 nanoparticles internalized by caveolin-1-dependent endocytosis, is proposed to engage two separable innate arms, one through stimulator of interferon genes 1 (STING1) yielding type I interferon and CXCL10, the other through NLRP3 and caspase - 1 yielding interleukin-1-beta; the first was shown in murine brain endothelium and the second in a human cerebral endothelial cell line, and the two have not been demonstrated in one system. Junctional remodeling and ephrin type-A receptor 2 signaling open the blood-brain barrier in murine models, barrier disruption is documented histologically in human autopsy series, and neuronal and axonal proteins reach the circulation of affected children. The sequence summarized here therefore combines links established in human disease with links that remain experimental or proposed, and the review marks which is which at each step. This review treats candidate biomarkers as readouts of that cascade rather than as free-standing correlates. Because the clinical definition cannot separate malaria-attributable coma from coma with incidental parasitemia, we appraise malarial retinopathy as the in vivo reference standard and set out why a negative result is heterogeneous. Parasite-derived and host-derived markers are mapped onto those steps, with attention to the few evaluated against non-malarial coma rather than against milder malaria, and to what a marker adds at the bedside. Extracellular vesicles and microRNAs are assessed as emerging platforms. We close on druggable nodes in the cascade and on using molecular readouts to stratify children for host-directed therapy.

43007365.resumo: Insect-pests remain a major constraint to global agriculture, causing yield losses through direct feeding and transmission of phytopathogens. Chemical pesticides and transgenic crops expressing Bacillus thuringiensis toxins have shown initial success; however, their use is increasingly constrained by resistance, non-target effects, environmental contamination and regulatory restrictions. Although RNA interference (RNAi) presents a targeted and eco-friendly alternative, it is limited by species variability, rapid double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) degradation, inconsistent silencing and off-target effects. Nuclease-active Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) enables genetic editing, but its irreversible genome modifications raise ethical, ecological and regulatory concerns. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) offers a programmable approach for sequence-specific, reversible transcriptional suppression without inducing double-strand DNA breaks. Using catalytically inactive Cas9 (dead Cas9 or dCas9) -guided by single-guide RNA (sgRNA), CRISPRi inhibits transcription initiation or elongation while maintaining genomic integrity. Experimental studies in insect models, including disease-vector mosquitoes, have demonstrated effective suppression of coding and non-coding genes, supporting CRISPRi as a functional genomics tool. This review discusses CRISPRi mechanisms, applications, advantages and limitations in insects, comparing it with RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9. Overall, current evidences indicate that CRISPRi is a precise and non-mutagenic platform for insect-pest management, particularly where controlled, reversible and species-specific gene regulation is desirable. However, its application in agricultural pest management remains an extrapolation from functional-genomics studies and requires validation in pest species under whole-organism and field-relevant conditions.

43007433.resumo: A central challenge in microbial ecology, particularly in engineered systems, is understanding how competing guilds coexist and why communities deviate from expected stability. Whereas polyphosphate accumulation provides energy and redox buffering in many heterotrophs, how lineages lacking polyphosphate synthesis manage equivalent redox imbalances remains an overlooked question. Using an enhanced biological phosphorus removal system, we integrated quantitative stoichiometry with metaproteomics to resolve alternative metabolic strategies that underpin cellular homeostasis in heterotrophs. We show that glycogen-accumulating organisms (Ca. Competibacter GAO) achieve stoichiometric yield parity with polyphosphate-accumulating organisms (Ca. Dechloromonas PAO) through a parallel redox-buffering mechanism: heterotrophic CO2/HCO3- assimilation via the ethylmalonyl-CoA pathway. This CO2/HCO3- fixation couples structural carbon conservation with tight redox control, mitigating intracellular electron overflow and eliminating the long-assumed GAO bioenergetic inferiority. The energetic efficiency of GAOs is further fortified by fine-tuned metabolic wiring, featuring energy-efficient high-affinity acetate activation, ferredoxin-mediated biochemistry, and ATP-neutral polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) mobilization. Metabolic parity is established between the two guilds growing on acetate, yet minor formate co-feeding tilts the delicate PAO-GAO balance. Formate supplementation creates an asymmetric bioenergetic niche that grants per-cycle energy gains primarily to GAOs. Decoupled from hydraulic throughput, solids retention time control retains cells carrying accumulated intracellular inventory, translating per-cycle energetic edges into a multi-generational ratchet that drives a community shift from PAO-GAO co-dominance to GAO dominance. By exposing limitations of traditional single-substrate and single-cycle steady-state models, our findings reveal how inorganic resource management and generational metabolic compounding shape community assembly in biomass-retaining microbial ecosystems.

43000516.resumo: Disulfidptosis is a newly recognized form of non-classical cell death, characterized by the abnormal accumulation of disulfide bonds and the collapse of the cytoskeleton. Nevertheless, the regulatory mechanisms governing this process are not fully understood. Although autophagy is a crucial cellular process necessary for maintaining homeostasis, its influence on the susceptibility to disulfidptosis and the associated mechanisms is currently unknown. This study primarily explored the interaction between autophagy and disulfidptosis in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells. In this research, both a pharmacological targeting model and a gene-modified model were established for functional and mechanistic assays. The impact of autophagy on disulfidptosis was assessed both in vitro and in vivo. Our findings revealed that the inhibition of autophagic flux significantly sensitized HCC cells to disulfidptosis through metabolic reprogramming, where the suppression of autophagy resulted in the downregulation of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) and impaired the generation of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate hydrogen (NADPH) and glutathione (GSH), which are critical for maintaining redox balance during disulfidptosis. Furthermore, the inhibition of autophagy also led to the suppression of mitophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction, which may further contribute to metabolic disruptions. Meanwhile, we identified endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress as an autophagy-dependent regulator of disulfidptosis, thereby establishing a comprehensive ER stress-autophagy-disulfidptosis axis. More importantly, we repurposed the clinical drug clofazimine as a novel disruptor of the equilibrium between ER stress and autophagy, which significantly enhances disulfidptosis in preclinical HCC models. These results improve our understanding of the regulation of disulfidptosis and provide evidence that autophagy acts as a principal suppressor of disulfidptosis, suggesting that pharmacological targeting of the homeostasis between ER stress and autophagy may represent a promising therapeutic approach for the treatment of HCC.

43000822.resumo: Hypophosphatemic rickets (HR) results from impaired renal phosphate reabsorption caused either by genetic defects in renal phosphate cotransporters or by increased levels of phosphaturic mediators (phosphatonins). Fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) is the principal regulator of phosphate metabolism and interacts with several hormonal and molecular pathways to maintain phosphate homeostasis. Variants in genes such as PHEX, FGF23, DMP1, ENPP1, FAM20C, and others lead to inherited forms of HR, and HR may also occur as part of several syndromic conditions. Affected patients typically present with short stature, skeletal deformities, bone pain, muscle weakness, dental abnormalities, and characteristic radiographic abnormalities. Laboratory findings usually include hypophosphatemia, normal or mildly elevated parathyroid hormone levels, and markedly increased alkaline phosphatase. Conventional therapy with oral phosphate and active vitamin D improves many metabolic abnormalities but rarely leads to full correction. The development of burosumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting FGF23, has transformed treatment by improving biochemical parameters, rickets severity, growth, and quality of life. This review summarizes current knowledge regarding the molecular mechanisms, clinical manifestations, diagnostic work-up, classification, and treatment strategies for HR, with particular emphasis on advances in targeted therapy.

43009957.resumo:
Timely treatment of malaria is critical to preventing severe disease and onward transmission. However, treatment-seeking behavior varies across populations and geographic settings. This study examined treatment-seeking time and its determinants among patients with confirmed malaria in Thailand using national surveillance data.
A retrospective analysis was conducted using surveillance data from laboratory-confirmed malaria cases recorded in Thailand's Electronic Malaria Information System (eMIS) from January 2012 to December 2024. The outcome was treatment-seeking time, defined as the number of days between the self-reported date of symptom onset and the date of confirmed malaria diagnosis recorded in the surveillance system. Descriptive statistics summarized treatment-seeking delays, while geographic variation was visualized using choropleth maps. Factors associated with treatment-seeking time were examined using negative binomial regression, with incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) reported.
A total of 127,242 confirmed malaria cases were analyzed. The majority were male (68.6%) and aged 15 years or older (73.5%), with Plasmodium vivax accounting for 75.0% of infections. The median treatment-seeking time was 2 days (interquartile range [IQR]: 1-3 days). Delays were longer among adults aged 15-34 years (IRR: 1.03; 95% CI 1.01-1.05) and ≥ 35 years (IRR: 1.03; 95% CI 1.01-1.05) compared with children under five years. Longer delays were also observed among long-term migrants (IRR: 1.04; 95% CI 1.03-1.06), short-term migrants (IRR: 1.06; 95% CI 1.04-1.08), and infections due to P. falciparum (IRR: 1.07; 95% CI 1.05-1.08), P. knowlesi (IRR: 1.19; 95% CI 1.12-1.26), and other species (IRR: 1.22; 95% CI 1.16-1.27), relative to P. vivax. Treatment-seeking time was longer in provinces classified as elimination-phase "clear-up" zones (IRR: 1.17-1.20) than in active transmission areas, whereas imported cases had shorter treatment-seeking times than indigenous cases (IRR: 0.96-0.98), likely reflecting differences in surveillance and case detection pathways. Western border provinces with historically high malaria burden showed relatively shorter treatment-seeking times.
Most individuals with confirmed malaria in Thailand were diagnosed within a relatively short period following symptom onset, although delays persisted among migrants, individuals with non-P. vivax infections, and residents of elimination-phase settings. Targeted interventions to improve access to care and awareness among mobile populations and low-transmission areas could further reduce treatment-seeking delays and support Thailand's malaria elimination goals.

43003214.resumo: Hsp90 is a molecular chaperone essential for the development of Plasmodium falciparum, the main agent of malaria. The emergence of drug-resistant malaria parasites continues to slow down efforts to control and eliminate the disease effectively. To mitigate antimalarial drug resistance, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends combination therapies. P. falciparum Hsp90 (PfHsp90) is an essential molecular chaperone. In addition, PfHsp90 is a promising antimalarial drug target, and its inhibition has been shown to reverse resistance to otherwise ineffective antimalarial drugs such as chloroquine. As such, understanding the functional features of PfHsp90 remains important for designing effective antimalarial therapies. In the current study, we expressed and purified recombinant PfHsp90 and investigated its interactions with one of its chaperone partners, PfHsp70, and a co-chaperone, PfHop, which brings the two chaperones into a functional complex to facilitate substrate exchange. Furthermore, we combined in silico and biochemical approaches to compare how PfHsp90 interacts with two known small-molecule inhibitors: geldanamycin and novobiocin. We demonstrated that both geldanamycin and novobiocin bind to PfHsp90 with higher apparent affinity than ATP. Furthermore, novobiocin registered a more dramatic conformational shift on PfHsp90 than geldanamycin. In addition, novobiocin more effectively inhibited the following functions of PfHsp90: self-association, co-chaperone (PfHop) binding, and holdase chaperone activity. We discuss the implications of our findings on the role of PfHsp90 and the prospect of this chaperone as an antimalarial drug target.

43012645.resumo: Malaria remains one of the world's most persistent infectious diseases, driven by complex interactions among human mobility, vector ecology, and environmental heterogeneity. Because mosquito larvae concentrate in aquatic habitats, biological control using larvivorous fish has long been used as a sustainable complement to insecticides. However, introducing predatory fish creates a central ecological trade-off where the same intervention that suppresses mosquito emergence also disrupts native aquatic communities. Addressing this concern, we develop a spatiotemporal eco-epidemiological framework that links vector-borne human pandemic spread, mosquito population movement and reproduction dynamics, and two interacting fish populations in which one intervention fish is introduced to consume larvae, and a native fish population is to be conserved. Within this framework, we compare a one-time offline deployment strategy with a dynamic monitoring strategy that updates fish release in response to local system states. Our results identify conditions under which adaptive deployment achieves a better balance between reducing human infections and preserving native fish, offering a principled basis for ecologically informed malaria control in heterogeneous urban landscapes. Quantitatively, both the offline and the monitoring strategy avert roughly two-thirds of the no-intervention infection burden and differ only modestly in epidemiological outcome. The monitoring strategy attains comparable infection control at a lower native-fish loss.

43009960.resumo:
The swift rise in pyrethroid resistance among malaria vectors poses a significant challenge to global malaria control. Although vector control tools have advanced, limited understanding of the vectorial capacity of highly pyrethroid-resistant mosquitoes hinders accurate predictions of how new interventions will affect malaria transmission in these resilient populations. Consequently, further research is needed to elucidate how escalating resistance influences mosquito vectorial capacity and shapes malaria transmission dynamics.
Wild Anopheles funestus s.l. mosquitoes were sampled from households in Adamaoua and Centre regions of Cameroon between February and September 2021 using a Prokopack aspirator. Phenotypic resistance to pyrethroids (permethrin, deltamethrin, alphacypermethrin) was assessed using WHO tube bioassays at diagnostic dose (DD), as well as at 5 × and 10 × DD. Plasmodium sporozoite infections were detected using TaqMan and nested PCR assays, and key resistance markers were genotyped by allele-specific PCR. Pearson's chi-squared tests and odds ratio were applied to examine the associations between resistance phenotypes, genotypes, and infection status.
Mosquitoes from Cameroon displayed low mortality rates in Mibellon, with only 33% mortality at the diagnostic dose (DD) and less than 95% mortality at 5 × and 10 × DD. In contrast, Elende populations exhibited lower resistance intensity. Sporozoite infection rates were very high in both collection sites (8.8% and 6% in Mibellon and Elende, respectively). Mosquitoes killed by elevated doses of type II pyrethroids were significantly more infected with Plasmodium than survivors (p < 0.05). Additionally, those surviving the highest deltamethrin doses showed reduced vectorial capacity compared to those surviving the 1 × diagnostic dose (OR = 2.8; 95% CI 1.1-7.3; p = 0.041). The persistence of elevated Plasmodium infection rates in mosquitoes surviving the highest permethrin concentrations underscores the direct impact of pyrethroid resistance escalation in driving malaria transmission. Genotypic analysis identified the L119F-GSTe2 mutation as associated with both resistance escalation and increased Plasmodium transmission whereas an opposite effect was observed for the P450 CYP9K1 with homozygote resistant 454A-CYP9K1 less infected than susceptible.
These findings highlight the urgent need for effective resistance management strategies to combat escalating pyrethroid resistance, while supporting the sustained use of type II pyrethroids, which remain effective against key Plasmodium-transmitting populations.

43003081.resumo:
Transfusion-transmitted malaria (TTM) is a rare but potentially severe transfusion complication. Increasing global mobility from malaria-endemic regions challenges donor selection policies in non-endemic settings, as asymptomatic parasitaemia may persist for years in previously exposed semi-immune individuals. This review aims to contextualise the residual risk of TTM and critically appraise current and past preventive strategies considering available evidence, with particular attention to policy implications.
A literature review of all confirmed cases of TTM reported in Europe and North America between 2005 and 2024 was performed to retrospectively assess the effectiveness and limitations of past and current preventive strategies, with particular reference to the recommendations of the European Directorate for the Quality of Medicines & HealthCare (EDQM) Blood Guide and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
Eighteen confirmed TTM cases were identified: 11 by Plasmodium falciparum with three fatalities, six by Plasmodium malariae and one by Plasmodium ovale. Sixteen cases were linked to donors born in or long-term residents of malaria-endemic regions, predominantly sub-Saharan Africa; two involved short-term European travellers. Since 2012, no P. falciparum TTM cases have been reported in Europe following the correct implementation of EDQM guidelines.
The residual risk of TTM in Europe and North America appears to be extremely low. However, long-term asymptomatic carriers-particularly of P. falciparum-remain a potential threat. Approaches based on deferral and immunological testing appeared to be effective and sustainable; nevertheless, high-sensitivity nucleic acid testing may represent a valuable alternative, particularly where blood availability is critical.

43010056.resumo:
Anopheles funestus, a major vector of malaria in Africa, has proven difficult to colonize in laboratory settings, impeding research on its biology and control. After several attempts, our team recently succeeded in colonizing a strain of An. funestus from Tanzania (FUTAZ). The objective of this study was to analyze the key fitness and genotypic characteristics of these mosquitoes during multiple filial generations of laboratory adaptation and compare them to wild An. funestus from Tanzania and a pre-existing colony of An. funestus from Mozambique (FUMOZ).
Measures of mating success, body size, fecundity, and insecticide resistance were compared between the newly established FUTAZ colonies, the long-established FUMOZ colonies, and a colony of Anopheles arabiensis maintained in the same laboratory. The maternal lineages of the An. funestus mosquitoes were investigated through a hydrolysis probe analysis of their mitochondrial DNA to identify distinct clades. Other intragenomic variations were examined by D3-RFLP genotyping of 28S ribosomal DNA. These molecular markers were used to compare the FUTAZ colonies, FUMOZ colonies in Tanzania (TZ) and South African (SA) laboratories, and the wild-collected Tanzanian An. funestus.
The mating success and body size of FUTAZ females declined significantly from filial generations F1 to F6 relative to the founder population (F0) then increased from F7 onwards, eventually matching FUMOZ by F9. Fecundity was similar across all colonies tested. However, it took significantly longer for 50% of the females in the FUTAZ and FUMOZ colonies (> 10 days) to mate compared to females in the An. arabiensis colony (~ 5 days). Resistance appeared to be lost during colonization, but this varied with insecticide classes. Majority of FUTAZ mosquitoes, and the wild-caught Tanzanian An. funestus belonged to Clade I (80.4-89.4%) and RFLP type "Y" (90.5-91.4%), while FUMOZ colonies in TZ and SA were mostly Clade II (65.5-88.5%) and RFLP type "MW" (90.5-91.5%).
This study demonstrates that certain fitness traits of An. funestus, notably mating success and body size, declined during the initial phases of laboratory colonization but recovered as the population adapted to laboratory conditions. Having large founder populations is critical to survive these early-generation bottlenecks. Clade-specific and RFLP genotyping confirmed FUTAZ colony as genetically representative of wild-caught Tanzanian An. funestus. This newly established colony constitutes a valuable and reliable resource for malaria vector research.

43008025.resumo: Nonchordate gap junction channels are formed by innexins, yet the structures and subunit assembly mechanisms of insect innexins remain unknown. We determined cryoelectron microscopy structures of AGAP001487, an innexin from the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae, reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs. The wild-type protein forms a rotationally symmetric heptameric hemichannel with an ordered N-terminal ring stabilized by intersubunit hydrogen bonds. Whereas deletion of a single N-terminal residue preserves channel activity, removal of two or more residues markedly impairs function. Consistent with these functional defects, the structure lacking two N-terminal residues exhibits disrupted rotational symmetry, extensive N-terminal disorder, pore collapse, and altered pore-lipid interactions. In addition, two-dimensional class averages revealed a minor population of hexameric particles, consistent with a potential assembly intermediate. Together, these structures support a stepwise assembly pathway in which intersubunit hydrogen bonding stabilizes N-terminal ring formation as a maturation step leading to a fully symmetric heptameric channel. Our findings identify N-terminal integrity as a critical determinant of oligomer maturation and channel function and provide mechanistic insight into how defined oligomeric assemblies are established in large-pore channel families.

43004473.resumo: Histone lactylation, particularly H3K18 lactylation (H3K18la), has emerged as a lactate-derived epigenetic modification that links metabolic reprogramming to sustained chromatin states. Here, we advance a hypothesis that the lactate-p300-H3K18la axis functions as an epigenetic memory code, converting transient glycolytic signals into persistent transcriptional responsiveness in innate immune cells-a mechanism we term "context-dependent lactylation memory." We integrate evidence from three converging domains: the persistence of lactylation at trained immune loci, the requirement of H3K18la for trained immunity demonstrated in recent BCG vaccination studies, and the hypoxic, glycolytic microenvironment of the atherosclerotic plaque. We propose that cardiovascular risk factors stabilize HIF-1α, which drives glycolytic reprogramming and sustained lactate production. Lactate-derived lactyl-CoA then serves as a substrate for p300/CBP-mediated H3K18la deposition at immune gene regulatory elements, creating a poised chromatin state that sustains innate immune hyperresponsiveness. This cascade provides a mechanistic explanation for residual inflammatory risk, the observation that elevated cardiovascular events persist despite optimal lipid-lowering therapy. Future studies combining longitudinal cohorts, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and multimodal biomarker strategies are needed to clarify causal relationships between glial states and AD progression and to facilitate translation toward precision classification and stage-specific intervention. This integrative perspective positions glial biomarkers as measurable links between cellular pathology and clinical evolution, offering a framework for mechanism-based patient stratification and therapeutic development.

The rise in HIV prevalence has led to more individuals using antiretroviral therapy (ART). These drugs, together with concurrent lifestyle factors, contribute to metabolic dysfunction, such as an increased risk of prediabetes. The asymptomatic nature of prediabetes may increase the probability of initiating ART without appropriate individualised regimen selection or required metabolic monitoring.
This study evaluated the effects of NRTI- and NNRTI-based fixed-dose combination regimens used as pre-exposure prophylaxis (Truvada) and for HIV management (Triovir) on selected markers of glucose homeostasis.

Prediabetes was induced using a high-fat, high-carbohydrate (HFHC) diet over 20 weeks, followed by a treatment period lasting 12 weeks. Treatment procedure: the NPD and PD rats were further randomly subdivided into their respective ART regimens (n = 7/group). After the treatment period, the study was terminated, and tissues and organs of interest were collected for biochemical analyses.
HFHC feeding effectively induced a PD phenotype, characterised by elevated fasting glucose, glucose intolerance, increased homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), hypertriglyceridaemia and weight gain (p < 0.05). Treatment with Truvada and Triovir attenuated these metabolic markers in PD and NPD groups. However, HOMA-IR was elevated in NPD animals following both treatments. The administration of either regimen in NPD animals increased plasma C-peptide levels, whereas plasma glucagon remained unchanged. In PD animals, Truvada treatment increased C-peptide concentrations, whereas Triovir reduced them. Hepatic glucose exhibited a pattern comparable with the C-peptide response in NPD animals. However, in PD groups, both treatments lowered glucagon levels and elevated hepatic glucose concentrations.
Truvada and Triovir caused mixed responses on metabolic dysfunction in diet-induced PD rats. These findings highlight the complex metabolic interactions of ART, warranting further mechanistic studies, particularly in populations on ART with pre-existing metabolic risk.

43005911.resumo: Diabetic foot ulcers are chronic wounds characterized by persistent inflammation, defective inflammatory resolution, and impaired tissue repair. Macrophages coordinate host defense, efferocytosis, inflammatory resolution, angiogenesis, and tissue reconstruction, but the diabetic wound environment can impair their adaptation, function, and survival. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by phospholipid peroxidation, has emerged as a potential mechanism linking diabetic wound stress to impaired macrophage function and survival. This review evaluates current evidence for ferroptosis in diabetic foot ulcers and distinguishes evidence from markers and pharmacological rescue obtained at the level of whole wounds from direct evidence in macrophages. We examine how altered iron handling and ferritinophagy, lipid remodeling, impaired glutathione peroxidase 4 activity and complementary antioxidant defenses, inflammatory and immunometabolic stress, and macrophage state may increase ferroptotic susceptibility. We then consider the potential consequences for macrophage functions required for repair, efferocytosis and inflammatory resolution, and support for fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and keratinocytes across wound regions and phases. Current studies support ferroptotic stress as a therapeutically modifiable process in diabetic wounds, but direct in situ evidence of ferroptotic stress or death in defined macrophage populations within human diabetic foot ulcers remains limited. Its biological consequences are also likely to vary according to macrophage state and wound phase. Accordingly, therapeutic strategies should avoid indiscriminate suppression or induction of ferroptosis and instead preserve macrophage functions required for antimicrobial defense, inflammatory resolution, and tissue repair while controlling excessive iron accumulation and phospholipid peroxidation. Spatially resolved biochemical analyses, longitudinal sampling, and functional perturbation in defined macrophage populations will be needed to establish causality and guide treatment according to macrophage state and wound phase.

43011492.resumo: Transition metals such as iron, zinc, and copper serve as indispensable cofactors in immunometabolic regulation. As central regulators of innate immunity, macrophages rely on strict metal homeostasis to maintain their functional plasticity. Studies have shown that transition metal dyshomeostasis is associated with aberrant macrophage polarization and sustained inflammatory responses. Such macrophage dysfunction may contribute to the initiation and progression of chronic systemic metabolic diseases. This review comprehensively summarizes the regulatory functions of essential transition metals in shaping macrophage inflammatory phenotypes and regulating metabolic reprogramming. We further clarify the molecular mechanisms by which metal-induced macrophage dysfunction participates in the pathogenesis of major metabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and atherosclerosis. We discuss how targeting intracellular metal homeostasis via selective metal chelators and novel metal-based nanomaterials represents a promising and innovative immunomodulatory therapeutic strategy. Essential transition metal homeostasis is a critical determinant of macrophage plasticity and appears to play a significant role in the pathogenesis of chronic metabolic diseases. Macrophage dysfunction induced by transition metal dyshomeostasis is associated with systemic insulin resistance and may contribute to tissue-specific damage within hepatic, vascular, and adipose microenvironments. Although the mechanistic foundations have been established, significant knowledge gaps remain regarding stage-specific variations and dose-dependent thresholds of metal-induced macrophage phenotypic shifts. Future research should prioritize the validation of metal-based biomarkers in clinical cohorts and the development of targeted 'metal-homeostasis' therapies to restore macrophage function, thereby providing a novel theoretical framework for the prevention and treatment of chronic metabolic disorders.

43003171.resumo: Atherosclerosis was traditionally viewed as a lipid-storage disorder driven by dyslipidemia and vascular injury. However, accumulating evidence indicates that immune mechanisms are central to disease initiation, progression, and plaque destabilization. Oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL) and related oxidation-specific epitopes (OSEs), ApoB100 peptides as well as newly identified autoantigens function as modified self-antigens that trigger both innate and adaptive immune responses, linking metabolic stress to chronic vascular inflammation. Innate immune activation is sustained through trained immunity, whereby monocytes and macrophages undergo long-lasting epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming that promotes a persistent pro-inflammatory phenotype. Additional contributors include dendritic cell-mediated antigen presentation, activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and interleukin-1β signaling pathway, and type I interferon responses, all of which amplify vascular inflammation and plaque progression. Clinical benefits observed with anti-inflammatory therapies targeting these pathways provide evidence for their pathogenic relevance. Adaptive immune responses are characterized by the presence of antigen-experienced T and B lymphocytes within atherosclerotic lesions. oxLDL- and apolipoprotein B (ApoB)-reactive T cells contribute to disease progression through loss of immune tolerance and predominance of pro-inflammatory T helper 1 responses, whereas regulatory T cells exert protective effects. CD8 cytotoxic T cells as well as B cell subsets contribute to the formation of atherosclerotic plaque. Humoral responses against oxLDL generate both atheroprotective and pro-inflammatory antibodies, depending on their specificity and functional properties. Emerging evidence of tertiary lymphoid structures within the arterial wall further supports local antigen-driven immune activation. The accelerated development of atherosclerosis in systemic autoimmune diseases highlights important mechanistic overlap between systemic autoimmunity and vascular pathology. Nevertheless, immune activation in atherosclerosis remains largely initiated by lipid accumulation and vascular injury rather than a primary breakdown of systemic immune tolerance. Atherosclerosis does not appear to require a primary, generalized breakdown of systemic self-tolerance. Nevertheless, ApoB-reactive CD4+ T cells can lose regulatory features during disease progression, indicating impaired antigen-specific immune regulation. Whether, and to what extent, the local arterial environment drives this change remains to be established. Collectively, current evidence supports the concept that atherosclerosis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease with prominent autoimmune features, providing a rationale for the development of targeted immunomodulatory therapies.

Human evidence is derived mainly from observational studies and secondary analyses of chronic GLP-1RA exposure, with limited evidence from trials initiating treatment during acute infection. Future translation will require cell-specific receptor validation, live-pathogen models with post-infection treatment, parallel assessment of pathogen control and host protection, clinically relevant standard-of-care comparators, and infection-specific safety evaluation. GLP-1RAs are therefore best regarded as candidate host-directed adjuncts. Current evidence does not establish them as direct anti-infective therapies.

43009129.resumo:
Systemic metabolic abnormalities are established drivers of cognitive decline, traditionally attributed to secondary sequelae of cerebrovascular dysfunction. However, cellular events linking early metabolic stress to subsequent neuronal injury and neurodegenerative processes remain poorly defined.
Here, we demonstrate that high-fat diet (HFD) triggers microglia to release pathogenic migrasomes (long-lived organelle-like vesicles) that promote neuronal injury, during an early phase of metabolic stress, before the emergence of overt dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia, and vascular pathology. We found that HFD feeding remodels the lipid environment of myelin-rich white matter and disrupts myelin homeostasis. Upon phagocytosis of this altered myelin, microglia generate migrasomes enriched with the neurotoxic alarmin S100A9. The pathogenicity of these vesicles was supported by complementary gain- and loss-of-function studies: intracerebral injection of HFD-induced microglial migrasomes was sufficient to impair cognition and induce neuronal injury in healthy mice, whereas Tspan9 conditional knockout in Cx3cr1-CreERT2 mice markedly reduced migrasome formation and thereby attenuated HFD-induced neurotoxicity. Dengue is a major public health concern in Southeast Asia, with increasing incidence and severity among adult populations. Early identification of factors associated with severe dengue is essential for timely clinical management and reducing morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to identify factors associated with severe dengue among adults hospitalized at a single tertiary center in Bangkok, Thailand.
A retrospective cohort study was conducted among adult patients (≥18 years) with laboratory-confirmed dengue who were hospitalized at Ramathibodi Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand, between January 2015 and December 2025. Patients were classified as severe or non-severe dengue according to the 2025 World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines. Factors associated with severe dengue were explored using multivariable logistic regression. Because of the small number of severe events, Firth's penalized logistic regression was applied to a reduced model with four covariates (age, diabetes mellitus, cough, and hepatosplenomegaly), with sensitivity analyses using an extended model and the full initial model.
A total of 143 patients were included (median age 36 years; 65.7% female); 21 (14.7%) developed severe dengue. More than half of the patients (52.4%) had underlying comorbidities, most commonly hypertension (31.5%) and dyslipidemia (30.1%), and 55.2% presented with WHO warning signs at admission. The most common severe dengue criteria were dengue shock syndrome (52.4%), aspartate transaminase (AST) or alanine transaminase (ALT) ≥1,000 U/L (28.6%), and severe bleeding (23.8%). In the primary Firth-penalized reduced model (143 patients; 21 events), hepatosplenomegaly (AOR 7.27, 95% CI 2.06-26.18; p=0.002) and cough at presentation (AOR 4.19, 95% CI 1.04-15.79; p=0.044) were associated with severe dengue, whereas the association with diabetes mellitus did not reach statistical significance (AOR 3.40, 95% CI 0.86-12.90; p=0.079). Hepatosplenomegaly remained significantly associated with severe dengue in all sensitivity analyses, whereas the association with cough was not consistent across models.
Among hospitalized adults with dengue, hepatosplenomegaly was consistently associated with severe dengue across standard and Firth penalized multivariable models. Associations with cough and diabetes mellitus were imprecise and sensitive to model specification. Given the small number of severe cases and single-center design, these findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger prospective cohorts.

Further investigations revealed that increased p-ERK was associated with global protein ubiquitination, suggesting this kinase as a key regulator of proteasomal degradation in diapause development. Our findings delineate a ROS-InR-IRS-Akt/ERK signaling framework associated with diapause development and proteostatic regulation in H. armigera, thereby advancing our understanding of insect diapause biology and providing candidate molecular targets for future pest-management interventions.

43009996.resumo:
Aedes aegypti is the primary vector of arboviruses of major public health importance which are spreading worldwide. Spinosad has been an important compound adopted for Ae. aegypti management, with selective larvicidal action based on the metabolites produced by the bacterium Saccharopolyspora spinosa. The expanding use of spinosad in mosquito control programs highlights the need for monitoring the potential development of resistance. This study evaluated the effects of continuous laboratory selection of an Ae. aegypti field-derived colony with spinosad, focusing on resistance development, cross-resistance patterns, and biological performance.
Ae. aegypti field sample from Recife city, Brazil, was used to establish the RecCam colony and the RecSpi strain. This strain was subjected to artificial selection with spinosad under controlled laboratory conditions for 20 generations, while RecCam was used as a reference colony for the study. Larvae susceptibility to spinosad and to other three larvicides, not used in selection process, was determined by in vivo assays. The biological fitness of RecSpi individuals was evaluated and compared to RecCam based on blood-feeding performance, fecundity, fertility, pre-imaginal development, adult production, and longevity assays.
The baseline susceptibility of the RecCam larvae to spinosad (LC₅₀ = 0.222 mg/L and LC₉₀ = 0.383 mg/L) was similar to another local reference colony (RecLab), while the Rockefeller colony exhibited the highest susceptibility (LC₅₀ = 0.160 mg/L, LC₉₀ = 0.265 mg/L). After 20 generations of spinosad selection, RecSpi larvae displayed a 9.7- and 8.5-fold resistance ratio at LC₅₀ (2.146 mg/L) and LC₉₀, (3.240 mg/L), compared to the RecCam reference, respectively. Notably, no cross-resistance was observed against Bacillus thuringiensis svar. israelensis (Bti), a combined larvicide based on Lysinibacillus sphaericus/Bti, or temephos. The RecSpi individuals displayed reduced biological performance characterized by prolonged larval development, reduced adult emergence, decreased adult longevity, and lowered blood intake compared to the RecCam strain.
Continuous selection with spinosad promoted resistance in Ae. aegypti RecSpi strain accompanied by a reduced biological performance. The absence of cross-resistance to commonly used larvicides underscores the unique spinosad mode of action and supports its use in rotation strategies. To maintain the efficacy of spinosad, resistance management approaches including rotational use and longitudinal susceptibility monitoring are necessary.

Despite this burden, no small-molecule antiviral has been approved for orthoflavivirus infections. Structure-activity relationship studies revealed a pronounced nucleobase dependence, with antiviral activity observed only among purine analogues. In contrast, pyrimidine analogues bearing 2'C-α-fluoro modifications were inactive in Vero cells. Combined with HINT1 kinetic analyses demonstrating poor processing of selected inactive AHA ProTides, these findings indicate that CES1 deficiency alone does not account for the lack of antiviral activity and highlight HINT1 substrate recognition as a critical determinant of successful prodrug activation. Among the compounds evaluated, AHA ProTide 5f showed the strongest activity against DENV-2 (EC50 = 22 ± 1 μM) and ZIKV (EC50 = 3 ± 2 μM) without detectable cytotoxicity up to 100 μM. Despite their biocontrol potential, species boundaries and phylogenetic relationships remain poorly understood. Utilizing country-wide sampling across Panama, we evaluated the taxonomic status and diversity of local Toxorhynchites species. 43010077.resumo:
In the past decade, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and reduced-representation genome sequencing of wild populations of the invasive mosquito species Aedes aegypti have identified genetic markers of vectorial capacity for arboviruses, such as DENV, host seeking behavior, and insecticide resistance. However, neither technique has been applied to Indian Ae. aegypti field isolates, despite India bearing a high annual arboviral burden.
To address this, we sequenced the whole genomes of eight Ae. aegypti mosquitoes sampled from dengue-endemic areas of Southern India and systematically investigated their genetic variability relative to the Ae. aegypti reference genome and global isolates using principal component analysis (PCA), ADMIXTURE, phylogenomics and other population statistical tests.

Next, to obtain a global view of Ae. aegypti population structure and evolutionary relatedness, the South-Indian genomes were compared to publicly available genomes of Ae. aegypti field isolates from different parts of the world. Based on PCA and ADMIXTURE, we observed that African Ae. aegypti samples clustered as a single group while the American, Samoan and Asian samples-inclusive of the ones from Southern India-formed a second group, but with distinct geographical sub-grouping and showed evidence of new admixing ancestries. Furthermore, phylogenomic analysis suggested a single out-of-Africa exit of Ae. aegypti with a subset of the Southern Indian isolates having diverged recently from other Asian populations.
Overall, our observations indicate ongoing genomic diversification of Ae. aegypti within Southern India, a factor that needs to be considered while designing vector control strategies such as insecticide-based control and those involving genetic modifications, such as gene drives.

Anti-Giardia IgM and IgG, multiplex cytokines, chemokines and growth factors, anthropometric measures, and metabolic parameters were assessed. Internal performance assessment using bootstrap resampling and stratified 10-fold cross-validation yielded similar estimates within the study cohort. Differences in apparent AUC between the integrated, immunological, and metabolic models were interpreted descriptively because no formal statistical comparison of ROC curves was performed.
In this study population, active G. intestinalis infection was associated with distinct immunological and metabolic patterns. The exploratory multivariable analysis identified a combination of immunological and metabolic variables with high apparent discriminatory performance within the present cohort. Biotransformation was investigated by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-positive electrospray ionization-Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (UHPLC-(+)ESI-Orbitrap/HRMS) and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), which allowed the tentative identification of metabolites, whereas the reduction of the parent compounds was estimated from chromatographic peak areas relative to abiotic controls. All strains grew in Luria-Bertani medium, but only three showed consistent growth in M9 minimal medium with the insecticides. Although Enterobacter asburiae P2D2C1 was also analyzed by GC-MS with deltamethrin, its profiles did not allow a reliable characterization of products; the final characterization therefore focused on Chryseobacterium gleum P31D2 (temephos) and Cedecea neteri P2HD2 (deltamethrin). After 72 h, C. gleum P31D2 reduced the temephos signal by 76.05% relative to the abiotic control, and five metabolites were tentatively identified, including 4,4'-thiodiphenol, 4,4'-sulfinyldiphenol, and temephos sulfoxide. C. neteri P2HD2 reduced the relative abundance of deltamethrin by 75.39% over 24 h versus 8.52% in the abiotic control (net biotransformation, 66.87%), and four metabolites were tentatively identified, including 3-phenoxybenzaldehyde and 3-phenoxyphenylacetonitrile. Hypothetical metabolic pathways are proposed. These in vitro findings provide a basis for future studies on the role of gut bacteria in insecticide biotransformation.

ensaio.historia:
Durante quase um século, a parasitologia molecular operou sob um dogma redutor: para entender por que um mosquito transmite ou bloqueia a malária, ou por que o camundongo desenvolve edema cerebral, deveríamos buscar sempre "o gene" ou "a citocina". Mapeamos vias inteiras (Toll, Imd, JAK-STAT), sequenciamos transcriptomas de células únicas e quantificamos centenas de RNAs mensageiros.

No entanto, uma pergunta desconfortável permaneceu sem resposta na bancada: **como decisões vitais de infecção ocorrem em frações de segundo, muito antes de qualquer RNA polimerase conseguir transcrever um gene?**

Quando o oocineto atinge o microvilo do mosquito, a digestão do sangue está no auge. Milhões de eritrócitos se rompem, gerando uma pressão coloidosmótica massiva, liberação letal de hemo livre e fluxo turbulento não-newtoniano. O parasito não tem horas para esperar uma via gênica ser ativada. Ele precisa explorar as propriedades biofísicas nativas do epitélio: diferenças de potencial elétrico entre células vizinhas, zonas de menor tensão mecânica e condensação líquida de proteínas de superfície.

Se quisermos descobrir o que não sabemos que existe, precisamos sair da nossa própria vizinhança conceitual. É no cruzamento com a biologia de sistemas de organelas, com a bioeletricidade do desenvolvimento e com a física da matéria mole que residem as próximas grandes viradas da nossa bancada.

grandes_pesquisadores.instituicao: Department of Molecular Genetics, Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot, Israel
grandes_pesquisadores.conceito_chave: Contactoma Celular & Comunicação Não-Vesicular de Organelas
grandes_pesquisadores.historia:
Maya Schuldiner revolucionou a biologia celular ao quebrar o paradigma de que as organelas intracelulares se comunicavam exclusivamente através de vesículas secretoras (via clássica de Golgi e retículo).

Usando triagem robótica em larga escala de leveduras (SGA - Synthetic Genetic Array) combinada com microscopia de fluorescência de altíssima resolução, seu laboratório no Weizmann descobriu que organelas como retículo endoplasmático, mitocôndrias, peroxissomos, gotas lipídicas e vacúolos estão fisicamente conectadas por pontes proteicas especializadas ("tethers"), formando uma malha contínua chamada de 'contactoma'. Essas fendas de 10 a 30 nanômetros permitem o transporte ultrarrápido de lipídios, íons cálcio e intermediários metabólicos vitais, operando como cabos de alta velocidade dentro da célula.

grandes_pesquisadores.conceito_chave: Bioeletricidade Morfogenética & Software Biológico de Tecidos
grandes_pesquisadores.historia:
Michael Levin é pioneiro na redefinição da biologia do desenvolvimento e regeneração: enquanto a maioria dos biólogos encara eletricidade celular como algo restrito a neurônios e músculos, Levin provou que **todas as células vivas mantêm gradientes bioelétricos de membrana (Vmem)** e se comunicam através de junções comunicantes (gap junctions).

Seu grupo demonstrou que redes bioelétricas funcionam como um 'software de alto nível' que define a morfologia anatômica, a regeneração de membros e o comportamento inflamatório, conseguindo induzir o crescimento de olhos funcionais em caudas de girinos ou reprogramar tecidos apenas alterando a condutância iônica local.

tecnicas_emergentes.tecnica: Espectroscopia AFM-IR em Nanoescala (Photo-Thermal Induced Resonance)
tecnicas_emergentes.o_que_e: Combinação de Microscopia de Força Atômica com Espectroscopia de Infravermelho (AFM-IR), permitindo caracterização química de espécies moleculares com resolução espacial de 10 a 20 nanômetros.
tecnicas_emergentes.historia:
Durante décadas, a espectroscopia de infravermelho clássica (FTIR) foi limitada pelo limite de difração da luz óptica (~2 a 10 micrômetros), sendo incapaz de identificar compostos químicos dentro de organelas isoladas.

O desenvolvimento do AFM-IR contornou esse limite físico ao utilizar a ponta ultrafina de um microscópio de força atômica para detectar a expansão térmica nanomecânica da amostra quando excitada por um laser infravermelho pulsado e sintonizável. Com isso, tornou-se possível obter o espectro de absorção química exato de nanodomínios lipídicos, agregados amiloides e depósitos minerais sem marcadores fluorescentes.
